title: Perfect charity casts out fear (1 John 4:18)

cards: A four-year-old stands at the edge of a swimming pool, toes curled over the side, shivering. In the water, her father holds out his arms. Jump, he says.
I've got you. She doesn't move. The water is deep and her stomach is a fist.
Then she looks at his face instead of the water, and something shifts. She jumps. What changed wasn't the depth of the pool.
It was where she was looking. Late in his first letter, John says something about fear that sounds almost too simple, until you watch a kid at the edge of a pool.

teach.b: The Douay-Rheims: "Fear is not in charity: but perfect charity casteth out fear, because fear hath pain. And he that feareth, is not perfected in charity."
Charity is the old word for love here, from the Latin caritas, the self-giving love the Greek calls agape. Perfect means grown up, complete, come to its full size.
And cast out is strong: the Greek says love throws fear outside, out the door. Why?

teach.h: FEAR HATH PAIN: WAITING FOR PUNISHMENT.
teach.b: Because, John says, fear hath pain. The Greek word points to punishment: the fear of someone waiting to be punished, who can't rest for wondering what's coming.
That's no way to live with God, and John says love is the way out. Just before this, he says God is love, and right after, that we love because he first loved us.
Fear goes when you look at his face instead of the water. Now, a careful point. The Catholic tradition doesn't say all fear of God disappears.
It speaks of fear of the Lord as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: awe, reverence, not wanting to hurt someone you love. What love casts out is the other kind, the cringing fear of a slave.
The Catechism borrows a picture from Saint Basil. You can stand before God like a slave, afraid of the whip.
Like a hired hand, working for wages.
Or like a child, who responds to the love of the one who first loved them. Only the third one jumps.

how: Catholics count fear of the Lord, understood as reverent awe, among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received at confirmation, and the Church teaches that love for God frees a person from the servile fear of punishment.

games.q: what does “perfect charity casts out fear” mean?
o: true believers never feel any fear at all
full-grown love throws out the fear of punishment
God's love removes all awe and reverence

games.q: love and fear — tap the pairs.
p: Saint Basil's three ways to stand

s: Catholic teaching says all fear of God should disappear
fear of the Lord, meaning awe and reverence, is one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. love casts out the fear of a slave.
in the Douay-Rheims, charity here means giving to the poor
it's the old word for love, from Latin caritas, the Greek agape.
John says fear has to do with punishment
fear hath pain: the Greek word points to punishment.

games.q: love is asking you to make a hard phone call. your stomach is a fist. what does John say happens as love grows?
o: the fear stays, and you learn to live with it.
full-grown love throws the fear out.
the fear is a sign you shouldn't call.
games.why: perfect charity casteth out fear. the Greek says love throws fear outside: it doesn't negotiate with it.

practice: What has love been asking of you that fear keeps blocking: a hard conversation, an apology, saying no to something that's hurting you?

Feel the fear, the toes over the edge, then look toward love instead of the water: the person, the good it would do. If you pray, look toward God, who first loved you; if not, picture the face that makes you brave.

wordCard.voice: Perfect charity casts out fear. First John four: full-grown love throws out the fear of punishment. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: perfect love (1 John 4:18). the Douay-Rheims, following Latin caritas, says perfect charity.

carryVoice: Your line: love casts out fear. And that's week eighty-eight: he hath care of you, be sober and watch, he is patient, seen and touched, he is faithful to forgive, in deed, and love casts out fear. Week eighty-eight, complete.
